content: The Queen Elizabeth Hospital in King’s Lynn, Norfolk, England, is an NHS District General Hospital situated on the eastern outskirts of the town. Its catchment area spans approximately 1,500 square kilometers and serves a population of around 250,000 people, covering West Norfolk, South Lincolnshire, and North East Cambridgeshire. The hospital has approximately 480 beds, though this number can vary due to financial constraints leading to ward closures. At full capacity, it can accommodate up to 574 beds. The hospital employs around 2,400 staff members and is supported by approximately 600 volunteers, making it the largest employer in the town. It is also a teaching hospital accredited by the University of East Anglia (UEA) in Norwich. Locally, it is often referred to as “The QE” or “The QEH.” Despite occasional misnaming as “The Queen Elizabeth II Hospital,” it is actually named after Queen Elizabeth The Queen Mother (Elizabeth Bowes-Lyon), not Queen Elizabeth II. The hospital site includes the main two-story hospital building, which opened in 1980. Additional facilities on the site include the Fermoy Unit, an adult mental health unit opened alongside the main hospital; the Arthur Levin Day Surgery Centre, which began operations on January 11, 1999; the Roxburgh Children’s Day Centre, which provides outpatient care for children; and the Phoenix Montessori Nursery. The Fermoy Unit and the Arthur Levin Day Surgery Centre are connected to the main hospital via a long service corridor. The site also houses staff residences and the BMI Sandringham Hospital, a private hospital operated by BMI Healthcare. Within the main hospital building, there is a small shop and a coffee bar for patients, visitors, and staff, located near the main entrance. However, the main hospital building is nearing the end of its functional lifespan and may require replacement in the near future, either on the current site or at a new location within the town. The hospital offers a wide range of medical services, including cardiology, dermatology, diabetic medicine, ENT, endocrinology, gastroenterology, general medicine, general surgery, geriatric medicine, gynecology, nephrology, neurology, ophthalmology, pediatric neurology, pediatrics, rheumatology, thoracic medicine, trauma and orthopedics, upper gastrointestinal surgery, and vascular surgery. It also has a full Accident and Emergency department and provides adult mental health services through the Fermoy Unit. Specialized services such as thoracic surgery, neurology, and plastic surgery are provided by the Norfolk and Norwich University Hospital in Norwich, while renal dialysis at the QEH is an outreach service from the nephrology department in Cambridge. The hospital is equipped with MRI and CT scanners for imaging and diagnostic purposes. It has seven operating theaters and 19 inpatient wards, all named after local villages and towns. As a teaching hospital, it includes facilities such as lecture theaters and two libraries for student use. Additionally, the hospital has a staff sports and social club on-site. The Healthcare Commission annually reviews hospitals based on two criteria: “Use of Resources” (financial performance) and “Quality of Service” (clinical performance). These are rated on a scale of “Weak,” “Fair,” “Good,” and “Excellent.” In the 2005/06 review, the Queen Elizabeth Hospital received a “Weak” rating for its use of resources due to significant debts but was rated “Good” for the quality of its services, reflecting strong clinical performance and acceptable waiting times. Despite financial challenges, the hospital has one of the highest patient satisfaction rates in the region, with 96% of patients treated within the four-hour guideline. The Arthur Levin Day Surgery Centre is consistently ranked among the best in the country, and the hospital has achieved notable success in reducing MRSA infection rates, thanks to research led by Professor Lyn Liebowitz. This research has contributed to a dramatic reduction in MRSA cases and is now being used to assist the Department of Health in reducing MRSA rates in other hospitals. The hospital has faced significant financial difficulties, with debts peaking at approximately £13 million in 2006. Efforts to reduce these debts have included unpopular measures such as ward closures, staff redundancies, increased parking charges, and extreme cost-cutting strategies like asking staff to take their litter home to reduce waste collection costs. Despite these measures, the hospital has been gradually reducing its debt. Historically, the Queen Elizabeth Hospital Trust and the Norfolk Primary Care Trust (PCT) have been underfunded by the government, contributing to the financial strain. In 2006, a local newspaper, the Lynn News, launched a fundraising appeal to build a helipad for the hospital. While the community successfully raised the required funds, the hospital considered selling the proposed helipad site to help pay off debts, causing controversy. Alternative sites for the helipad were proposed but faced higher development costs and planning permission refusals. In April 2007, the potential buyer for the land withdrew, and the hospital decided to proceed with building the helipad on the originally proposed site. The hospital is currently applying for Foundation Trust status, which, if granted, would provide greater control over its finances and operations. This status could be achieved as early as 2008. Notable individuals associated with the Queen Elizabeth Hospital include Colin Bone, a consultant gynecologist who underwent gender reassignment surgery and returned to work as Celia Macleod. This event received national attention and was well-received by hospital staff and patients. Both Queen Elizabeth II and Queen Elizabeth The Queen Mother have received treatment at the hospital. The Queen Mother was treated there in February 1998 after fracturing her hip at Sandringham and again in January 1999 for recurrent nosebleeds, during which her nose was cauterized. Queen Elizabeth II was treated at the hospital in January 2003 for knee problems, where a scan was performed before she was transferred to the King Edward VII Hospital in London for surgery to remove torn cartilage. Various members of the Royal Family have visited the hospital over the years, including Princess Anne, who opened the £5 million Critical Care Unit in 2005.
